metadata.chapter_title: Geometric Proofs, Circle Geometry, and Networks (10 & 10A)
metadata.title: [10A] Circle Geometry: Angle, Chord, and Tangent Theorems
metadata.vcaa_description: Prove and apply angle and chord properties of circles, and tangent and secant properties of circles (VC2M10ASP02).
metadata.target_mastery: Prove and apply circle theorems including angle at the centre ($2\theta$), angle in a semicircle ($90^\circ$), angles in the same segment, cyclic quadrilaterals, tangent-radius perpendicularity, the alternate segment theorem, and intersecting chords/secants/tangents.
prerequisites: Deductive geometric proofs and triangle congruence (Section 7A)
Isosceles triangle and exterior angle properties

key_vocabulary.term: Subtended angle at the centre and circumference
key_vocabulary.definition: The angle formed by rays joining the endpoints of an arc $AB$ to the centre $O$ ($\angle AOB$) or to a point $P$ on the remaining circumference ($\angle APB$), related by $\angle AOB = 2\angle APB$.

A four-sided polygon whose four vertices all lie on the circumference of a single circle; its opposite interior angles are always supplementary ($\alpha + \gamma = 180^\circ$ and $\beta + \delta = 180^\circ$).

A tangent line touches a circle at a single point of contact $T$ and is perpendicular to the radius $OT$ ($90^\circ$). The angle between a tangent and a chord at $T$ equals the angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment.

key_vocabulary.term: Intersecting chords, secants, and tangent power theorems
key_vocabulary.definition: When two chords $AB$ and $CD$ intersect at $X$, $AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD$; for an external point $P$ with tangent $PT$ and secant $PAB$, $PT^2 = PA \cdot PB$.

theory.title: Angle Properties of Circles: Centre, Semicircle, Same Segment, and Cyclic Quadrilaterals
theory.explanation: Four foundational circle angle theorems all stem from the isosceles radii triangles $\triangle OAP$ and $\triangle OBP$ inside a circle of centre $O$: (1) The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc ($\angle AOB = 2\angle APB$). (2) As a special case when $AB$ is a diameter ($\angle AOB = 180^\circ$), the angle in a semicircle is a right angle ($\angle APB = 90^\circ$, Thales' theorem). (3) Angles in the same segment subtended by the same arc are equal ($\angle APB = \angle AQB$). (4) The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$ (supplementary), and an exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.
theory.callout_rule: Every radius of a circle has the same length $r$. Whenever two radii $OA$ and $OB$ form a triangle $\triangle OAB$, it is automatically isosceles with equal base angles ($\angle OAB = \angle OBA$).

theory.title: Chord Properties and Tangent Theorems
theory.explanation: A perpendicular drawn from the centre $O$ to a chord $AB$ always bisects the chord ($AM = MB$) and bisects the central angle $\angle AOB$. For a tangent line touching a circle at point $T$: (1) the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact ($\angle OTP = 90^\circ$), (2) two tangents drawn to a circle from the same external point $P$ have equal lengths ($PA = PB$, proved by $\triangle OAP \equiv \triangle OBP$ via RHS), and (3) by the Alternate Segment Theorem, the angle between a tangent at $T$ and a chord $TA$ equals the angle $\angle TBA$ subtended by $TA$ in the alternate segment.
theory.formula_latex: OT \perp \text{tangent at } T \ (90^\circ), \qquad PA = PB, \qquad \angle(\text{tangent},\, TA) = \angle TBA
theory.callout_title: Tangent-Chord Angle = Angle in the Alternate Segment
theory.callout_rule: In the Alternate Segment Theorem, look for a triangle inscribed in the circle with one vertex touching a tangent line: the angle between the tangent and one side equals the interior angle opposite that side.

theory.title: Intersecting Chords, Secants, and Tangent-Secant Power Theorems (VC2M10ASP02)
theory.explanation: Using similar triangles (AAA similarity from angles in the same segment or alternate segment theorem), we obtain three multiplicative length theorems for lines meeting a circle: (1) Intersecting Chords Theorem: if chords $AB$ and $CD$ cross internally at $X$, then $AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD$. (2) Intersecting Secants Theorem: if two secants from an external point $P$ cut the circle at $A, B$ and $C, D$ respectively, then $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$ (always multiply the outside segment by the WHOLE secant length from $P$!). (3) Tangent-Secant Theorem: if $PT$ is a tangent and $PAB$ is a secant from $P$, then $PT^2 = PA \cdot PB$.
theory.formula_latex: AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD, \qquad PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD, \qquad PT^2 = PA \cdot PB
theory.callout_rule: When a secant $PAB$ is drawn from an external point $P$, the product is $PA \times PB$ (outside part $\times$ total length from $P$ to the far intersection $B$), NEVER $PA \times AB$.

worked_examples.title: Applying Angle at the Centre, Same Segment, and Cyclic Quadrilaterals
worked_examples.problem: (a) Points $A, B, C, D$ lie on a circle with centre $O$ such that $A, B$ are joined to $O$ with $\angle AOB = 116^\circ$, and $C$ lies on the major arc $AB$ while $D$ lies on the minor arc $AB$. Find $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$. (b) If $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $P$ is a point on the circumference with $\angle PAB = 37^\circ$, find $\angle PBA$.

steps.thinking: In (a), the angle at the centre $\angle AOB = 116^\circ$ is twice the angle $\angle ACB$ at the circumference on the major arc.
Since $ACBD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, its opposite angles $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$ are supplementary ($\text{sum} = 180^\circ$).
In (b), since $AB$ is a diameter, $\angle APB = 90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). Use the angle sum of $\triangle APB$.

now_you_try.problem: In a cyclic quadrilateral $PQRS$, $\angle P = 78^\circ$ and $\angle Q = 105^\circ$. Find the sizes of the opposite interior angles $\angle R$ and $\angle S$.
now_you_try.hint: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$.

worked_examples.title: Chord Distance from Centre and Tangent Lengths from an External Point
worked_examples.problem: (a) A circle of radius $r = 13\text{ cm}$ has a chord $AB$ of length $24\text{ cm}$. Find the perpendicular distance $d = OM$ from the centre $O$ to the chord $AB$. (b) From an external point $P$ located $17\text{ cm}$ from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $8\text{ cm}$, two tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn to the circle. Find the length of each tangent.

steps.thinking: In (a), the perpendicular from the centre $O$ to the chord $AB$ bisects the chord at $M$, so $AM = \frac{24}{2} = 12\text{ cm}$. Apply Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled $\triangle OMA$ with hypotenuse $OA = 13\text{ cm}$.
In (b), the radius $OA = 8\text{ cm}$ is perpendicular to the tangent $PA$ at $A$ ($\angle OAP = 90^\circ$), so $OP = 17\text{ cm}$ is the hypotenuse of right-angled $\triangle OAP$.

now_you_try.problem: A chord lies at a perpendicular distance of $6\text{ cm}$ from the centre of a circle of radius $10\text{ cm}$. Find the total length of the chord.
now_you_try.hint: Find half the chord length $\sqrt{10^2 - 6^2}$ first, then double it.

worked_examples.title: Intersecting Chords and Tangent-Secant Power Theorems
worked_examples.problem: (a) Two chords $AB$ and $CD$ intersect at point $X$ inside a circle such that $AX = 6\text{ cm}$, $XB = 8\text{ cm}$, and $CX = 4\text{ cm}$. Find the length of $XD$. (b) From an external point $P$, a tangent $PT$ and a secant $PAB$ are drawn to a circle. Given that the external segment is $PA = 4\text{ cm}$ and the internal chord segment is $AB = 5\text{ cm}$, find the length of the tangent $PT$.

steps.thinking: In (a), apply the Intersecting Chords Theorem $AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD$.
In (b), first find the whole secant length $PB = PA + AB = 4 + 5 = 9\text{ cm}$, then apply the Tangent-Secant Theorem $PT^2 = PA \cdot PB$.

now_you_try.problem: From an external point $P$, two secants $PAB$ and $PCD$ are drawn to a circle. Given $PA = 5\text{ cm}$, $AB = 7\text{ cm}$, and $PC = 4\text{ cm}$, find the internal chord length $CD$.
now_you_try.hint: Use $PA \cdot PB = PC \cdot PD$ where $PB = 5 + 7 = 12\text{ cm}$ and $PD = 4 + CD$.

common_misconceptions.title: Multiplying Outside $\times$ Inside ($PA \times AB$) Instead of Outside $\times$ Whole ($PA \times PB$) for Secants
common_misconceptions.misconception: In the secant theorems, multiplying the external segment $PA$ by the internal chord $AB$ instead of the total secant length $PB = PA + AB$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: In the similar triangles $\triangle PAT \sim \triangle PTB$, the side lengths measured from vertex $P$ are $PA$, $PT$, and the entire secant $PB = PA + AB$. Therefore $PT^2 = PA \cdot (PA + AB)$.
common_misconceptions.incorrect_working: $$PA = 4,\, AB = 5: \quad PT^2 = 4 \times 5 = 20 \quad \text{(Incorrect — used } AB \text{ instead of } PB = 9\text{)}$$
common_misconceptions.counter_example: If the internal chord shrinks to $AB = 0$ (so the secant becomes a tangent), $PB = PA$ and $PT^2 = PA \cdot PB = PA^2$ holds true, whereas $PA \cdot AB$ would give $0$.

common_misconceptions.title: Assuming Opposite Angles of a Cyclic Quadrilateral Are Equal Instead of Supplementary
common_misconceptions.misconception: Confusing a cyclic quadrilateral with a parallelogram and setting opposite angles equal ($\alpha = \gamma$) instead of summing them to $180^\circ$ ($\alpha + \gamma = 180^\circ$).
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral subtend complementary arcs that together form the full $360^\circ$ circle at the centre, so the circumference angles sum to $\frac{360^\circ}{2} = 180^\circ$.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal ONLY when both equal $90^\circ$ (a rectangle inscribed in a circle).

fluency_and_understanding.question: An arc $AB$ of a circle with centre $O$ subtends an angle of $\angle APB = 34^\circ$ at a point $P$ on the major arc and $\angle AQB$ at another point $Q$ on the same major arc. Find (a) $\angle AQB$, and (b) the central angle $\angle AOB$.
step_by_step_solution: Angles in the same segment are equal: $\angle AQB = \angle APB = 34^\circ$.
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference: $\angle AOB = 2 \times 34^\circ = 68^\circ$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: In a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle DAB = 3x + 10^\circ$ and the opposite angle is $\angle BCD = 2x + 20^\circ$. Find the value of $x$ and the size of $\angle DAB$.
step_by_step_solution: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: $(3x + 10) + (2x + 20) = 180$.
Solve $5x + 30 = 180 \implies 5x = 150 \implies x = 30^\circ$, so $\angle DAB = 3(30^\circ) + 10^\circ = 100^\circ$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: A tangent line touches a circle at point $T$, and a chord $TA$ makes an acute angle of $62^\circ$ with the tangent. Point $B$ lies on the major arc $TA$ so that $\triangle TAB$ is inscribed in the circle with $\angle TAB = 48^\circ$. Find (a) $\angle TBA$ using the Alternate Segment Theorem, and (b) $\angle ATB$.
step_by_step_solution: By the Alternate Segment Theorem, the angle in the alternate segment equals the tangent-chord angle: $\angle TBA = 62^\circ$.
By the angle sum of $\triangle TAB$, $\angle ATB = 180^\circ - (48^\circ + 62^\circ) = 70^\circ$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Two chords $AB$ and $CD$ intersect internally at $X$ inside a circle. Given $AX = 9\text{ cm}$, $XB = 4\text{ cm}$, and $CX = XD = x\text{ cm}$, find the value of $x$ and the total length of chord $CD$.
step_by_step_solution: By the Intersecting Chords Theorem, $AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD \implies 9 \times 4 = x^2$.
Take the positive square root: $x = \sqrt{36} = 6\text{ cm}$, so $CD = 2x = 12\text{ cm}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: An archeologist discovers a broken circular ceramic plate. A straight chord $AB$ across the fragment measures $16\text{ cm}$, and the perpendicular height (sagitta) from the midpoint $M$ of the chord to the outer rim arc is $4\text{ cm}$. Use the Intersecting Chords Theorem on the full diameter perpendicular to $AB$ to find the radius $r$ of the original unbroken plate.
step_by_step_solution: Let the diameter perpendicular to $AB$ at its midpoint $M$ have segments of length $4\text{ cm}$ and $(2r - 4)\text{ cm}$, while $AM = MB = 8\text{ cm}$.
By the Intersecting Chords Theorem, $4(2r - 4) = 8 \times 8 = 64 \implies 2r - 4 = 16 \implies 2r = 20 \implies r = 10\text{ cm}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: Two tangents $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn from an external lighthouse beacon $P$ to a circular reef of centre $O$. If the angle between the two tangents is $\angle APB = 50^\circ$, find (a) the central angle $\angle AOB$ subtended by the points of contact, and (b) the base angle $\angle OAB$ inside $\triangle OAB$.
step_by_step_solution: In quadrilateral $OAPB$, the tangent-radius angles are $\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ$, so $\angle AOB = 360^\circ - (90^\circ + 90^\circ + 50^\circ) = 130^\circ$.
Since $OA = OB$ (radii), $\triangle OAB$ is isosceles with $\angle OAB = \frac{180^\circ - 130^\circ}{2} = 25^\circ$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A satellite $P$ orbits at an altitude of $h = 3600\text{ km}$ above the surface of a spherical planet of radius $R = 5400\text{ km}$. Use the Tangent-Secant Theorem $PT^2 = PA \cdot PB$ (where $PA = h$ and $PB = h + 2R$) to find the straight-line tangent distance $PT$ from the satellite to the planet's horizon.
step_by_step_solution: The secant line passing through the planet's centre has near distance $PA = h = 3600\text{ km}$ and far distance $PB = h + 2R = 3600 + 10\,800 = 14\,400\text{ km}$.
By the Tangent-Secant Theorem, $PT^2 = PA \cdot PB = 3600 \times 14\,400 = 51\,840\,000 \implies PT = \sqrt{51\,840\,000} = 7200\text{ km}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A circular tunnel has a diameter $AB = 10\text{ m}$. A maintenance platform $P$ on the semicircular roof ceiling is positioned $6\text{ m}$ in a straight line from end $A$ ($AP = 6\text{ m}$). Find (a) the straight-line distance $BP$ to the other end $B$, and (b) the vertical height $h$ of the platform $P$ above the horizontal floor $AB$.
step_by_step_solution: By Thales' theorem (angle in a semicircle), $\angle APB = 90^\circ$, so $BP = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = 8\text{ m}$.
Equating the area of $\triangle APB$ in two ways ($\frac{1}{2} \times AP \times BP = \frac{1}{2} \times AB \times h$) gives $6 \times 8 = 10h \implies h = 4.8\text{ m}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Prove the Angle at the Centre Theorem ($\angle AOB = 2\angle APB$) by drawing the radius ray $PO$ extended to $X$ and applying the isosceles triangle and exterior angle theorems to $\triangle OAP$ and $\triangle OBP$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: In isosceles $\triangle OAP$ ($OA = OP$), let $\angle OPA = \alpha \implies \text{exterior } \angle AOX = 2\alpha$; in isosceles $\triangle OBP$ ($OB = OP$), let $\angle OPB = \beta \implies \text{exterior } \angle BOX = 2\beta$; adding gives $\angle AOB = 2(\alpha + \beta) = 2\angle APB$
step_by_step_solution: Since $OA = OP$ (radii), $\triangle OAP$ is isosceles with $\angle OAP = \angle OPA = \alpha$, so the exterior angle at $O$ is $\angle AOX = \alpha + \alpha = 2\alpha$.

Similarly, $OB = OP$ makes $\triangle OBP$ isosceles with $\angle OBP = \angle OPB = \beta$ and exterior angle $\angle BOX = 2\beta$, so $\angle AOB = 2\alpha + 2\beta = 2(\alpha + \beta) = 2\angle APB$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Use the Angle at the Centre Theorem (including reflex angles at $O$) to prove that the opposite interior angles $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ of any cyclic quadrilateral sum to $180^\circ$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: The central angles subtended by the two opposite arcs are $2\alpha$ and $2\gamma$; since they form a full revolution around $O$, $2\alpha + 2\gamma = 360^\circ \implies \alpha + \gamma = 180^\circ$
step_by_step_solution: Join opposite vertices $B$ and $D$ to the centre $O$; by the Angle at the Centre Theorem, the two central angles around $O$ are $2\alpha$ and $2\gamma$.
Angles at a point sum to $360^\circ$: $2\alpha + 2\gamma = 360^\circ \implies \alpha + \gamma = 180^\circ$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Prove the Intersecting Chords Theorem ($AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD$) for two chords $AB$ and $CD$ intersecting at $X$ by proving that $\triangle AXC \sim \triangle DXB$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: $\angle AXC = \angle DXB$ (vertically opposite) and $\angle CAX = \angle BDX$ (angles in same segment on arc $BC$) $\implies \triangle AXC \sim \triangle DXB$ (AAA) $\implies \frac{AX}{DX} = \frac{CX}{XB} \implies AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD$
step_by_step_solution: In $\triangle AXC$ and $\triangle DXB$, $\angle AXC = \angle DXB$ (vertically opposite) and $\angle CAX = \angle BDX$ (angles in the same segment subtended by arc $BC$), so $\triangle AXC \sim \triangle DXB$ (AAA).
Equating ratios of matching sides gives $\frac{AX}{DX} = \frac{CX}{XB}$, which cross-multiplies to $AX \cdot XB = CX \cdot XD$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Prove that if a parallelogram $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle (i.e. is a cyclic parallelogram), then $ABCD$ must be a rectangle.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal ($\angle A = \angle C$), and in a cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles sum to $180^\circ$ ($\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$), so $2\angle A = 180^\circ \implies \angle A = \angle B = \angle C = \angle D = 90^\circ$ (a rectangle)
step_by_step_solution: Because $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal ($\angle A = \angle C$ and $\angle B = \angle D$).

Because $ABCD$ is cyclic, opposite angles are supplementary ($\angle A + \angle C = 180^\circ$), so $2\angle A = 180^\circ \implies \angle A = \angle C = 90^\circ$ and similarly $\angle B = \angle D = 90^\circ$, proving $ABCD$ is a rectangle.
